detailed_rationale:
Adani Green Energy is India's largest renewable-energy generator and, on pure execution, one of the best in the world right now: FY26 operational capacity grew 35% YoY to 19.3 GW (5.1 GW of greenfield additions in the year, the highest globally outside China), and the company crossed 20 GW (20,142 MW, +27% YoY) in its Q1 FY27 provisional operational update released early July 2026. FY26 power-supply revenue was Rs 11,602 crore (+22% YoY) with EBITDA of Rs 10,865 crore (+23% YoY) at an industry-leading 91% margin, and the flagship Khavda site (a planned 30 GW park, the largest RE project site in the world) is already >30% built out. Full financial results for the June-2026 quarter (Q1 FY27) are NOT yet out as of today (board meeting scheduled 22-Jul-2026) - only the operational (capacity/energy-sales) update has been released, so this call is built on the audited FY26/Q4FY26 print plus that provisional operating data, not on Q1 FY27 P&L.

The balance sheet is where the story turns. Net debt grew Rs 26,790 crore in FY26 alone to Rs 91,252 crore - roughly 4.2-4.6x book equity (Rs 19,965 crore) and about 8.4x FY26 delivered EBITDA (management prefers a 'run-rate EBITDA' of Rs 16,155 crore, which would put it near 5.6x, but that run-rate number annualizes capacity that was only commissioned partway through the year and has not yet been earned). Q4 FY26 interest cost was Rs 1,626 crore, up 18.9% YoY and consuming ~46% of net sales; EBIT/interest coverage sits at roughly 1.1x-1.7x depending on the quarter and consolidation basis used (quant context had 1.66x; the Q4 print alone computes closer to 1.1x) - either way, coverage is thin for a company still adding Rs 40,000-45,000 crore of FY27 capex, almost entirely debt-funded. Earnings quality also had rough edges in FY26: Q3 FY26 was reportedly a net loss (~Rs 41 crore per one aggregator) before Q4 recovered to Rs 397-514 crore (aggregators disagree on the exact PAT figure - a genuine data inconsistency across sources, flagged rather than papered over), and Q4 other income of Rs 225 crore was ~38% of PBT - most likely treasury/interest income on cash balances rather than a divestment gain (no asset-sale was reported in FY26 news flow), but it is a recurring-quality question worth carrying forward, not a clean operating print.

The renewables-specific risk here is not classic discom-counterparty risk - AGEL itself disclosed that ~Rs 1,200-1,500 crore of FY26 earnings were foregone not because customers didn't pay, but because grid-evacuation infrastructure (Central Transmission Utility readiness) lagged commissioning, forcing roughly Rs 500 crore of curtailment losses and Rs 800-1,000 crore of power sold on the merchant market below contracted PPA rates. Management's own response - deliberately capping additions at 4.5-5 GW/year versus an admitted 7-8 GW/year capital capacity, to match grid readiness - confirms the growth algorithm is now infra-gated, not capital-gated. That is a structural crack in the 'PPA-backed cash-flow visibility' thesis that a renewables analyst has to price in, separate from any discom-receivables discussion (SECI/NTPC contracts carry payment-security-fund protection; state discom exposure is a separate, generally smaller book). On governance, the picture actually improved materially this year: the Nov-2024 US DOJ bribery indictment against Gautam Adani, Sagar Adani and others (which specifically cited AGEL's 2021 $750mn bond-offering documents) became the subject of a DOJ motion to dismiss with prejudice on 18-May-2026 (court approval still pending as of mid-July 2026), alongside a proposed token SEC civil settlement ($6mn + $12mn, no admission of wrongdoing); promoter pledge on AGEL has been at 0.0% since mid-2024 (from 3.35% in Sep-2023); and JCR assigned an inaugural sovereign-equivalent BBB+/Stable rating in FY26. Governance overhang is genuinely lower today than a year ago - it just isn't the reason to buy a 130-155x P/E, 12.5x P/B compounder with 1.1-1.7x interest coverage.
recommendation_rationale: This is a Sell, not because AGEL executes poorly - it doesn't, capacity delivery is best-in-class - but because the price already embeds near-flawless multi-year execution while the balance sheet embeds real fragility. ROE (11.4% 1yr / 13.4% 3yr) and ROCE (~7.4-9%) are ordinary-to-weak for an asset-heavy utility-style business, yet the stock trades at ~120-155x trailing P/E (source-dependent) and 12.5x book - a combination that only works if earnings compound at a rate the current coverage ratio (1.1-1.7x EBIT/interest) and evacuation-bottleneck-constrained growth pace cannot comfortably deliver without further leverage. Quant's own model independently flags this: bs_flag RED and Reduce on both the 1y and 3y recommendation. A Hold would require either a materially cheaper entry multiple or visible deleveraging/coverage improvement; neither is present, and FY27 guidance (another Rs 40,000-45,000cr of capex) points to leverage rising further, not falling. This is a valuation/balance-sheet call, not a business-quality call, and it is clear-cut enough that it does not need an FM coin-flip ruling.
summary: Adani Green is India's biggest renewable-power generator and is genuinely executing well - it added more clean-energy capacity in FY26 than almost any company outside China and just crossed 20 GW operational scale. But the stock's price already assumes years of near-perfect growth, while the balance sheet tells a more stressed story: debt grew by nearly Rs 27,000 crore in a single year, interest costs are eating close to half of quarterly sales, and the profit-coverage cushion is razor-thin. On top of that, the company itself disclosed it lost Rs 1,200-1,500 crore of potential FY26 earnings because the power grid could not keep pace with the new capacity it built, forcing it to sell some power at a discount on the open market instead of at contracted rates. Governance risk has genuinely eased this year - the US bribery case against the promoters was permanently dropped in May 2026 and pledged shares are at zero - but at roughly 130-plus times earnings and 12.5 times book value, this is priced for perfection that a thinly-covered, still-heavily-levered balance sheet cannot comfortably guarantee. We rate it a Sell on valuation-versus-balance-sheet risk, not on the quality of the underlying business.
positive_para: AGEL is the scale leader in Indian renewables and it keeps proving it can build: 5.1 GW of greenfield capacity added in FY26 alone (a global high outside China), 19.3 GW operational at FY26-end rising to over 20 GW by Q1 FY27, and a credible line of sight to its own 50 GW-by-2030 target anchored by the 30 GW Khavda mega-site, already >30% built. Power-supply EBITDA margins of 91% are best-in-class for the sector, PPA fulfilment ran at 106% of annual commitments in FY26, and the company is diversifying into storage (BESS) ahead of most peers, which should help monetize otherwise-curtailed generation over time. Governance risk, long an overhang on the whole Adani complex, has eased materially in 2026: the DOJ moved in May 2026 to dismiss the criminal US bribery indictment against Gautam Adani and Sagar Adani with prejudice (court approval still pending), the parallel proposed SEC settlement is modest and admission-free, promoter pledge on AGEL shares has been zero since mid-2024, and the company picked up an inaugural sovereign-equivalent (JCR BBB+/Stable) credit rating this year.
negative_para: The balance sheet is the strongest argument against paying up here. Net debt rose by Rs 26,790 crore in FY26 to Rs 91,252 crore - about 4.2-4.6x book equity - while EBIT/interest coverage sits at only 1.1x-1.7x, meaning operating profit barely clears the interest bill in a company still guiding to another Rs 40,000-45,000 crore of FY27 capex, funded overwhelmingly by more debt. Returns on capital (ROCE ~7.4-9%, ROE ~11-13%) are unremarkable for an asset-heavy business trading at 12.5x book value and 120-155x earnings - a multiple that assumes many years of uninterrupted, high-teens-to-20s compounding. That assumption is now visibly strained: management itself disclosed Rs 1,200-1,500 crore of FY26 earnings foregone because grid-evacuation infrastructure could not absorb the new capacity as fast as it was built, forcing curtailment and below-PPA merchant sales, and it has deliberately throttled additions to 4.5-5 GW/year versus an admitted achievable 7-8 GW/year purely to wait for the grid - an infra ceiling AGEL cannot capex its way past. Earnings quality also wobbled through FY26 (a reported Q3 loss before a Q4 recovery, and Q4 other income near 38% of PBT), and reported PAT figures for the same quarter disagree meaningfully across data aggregators, which is itself a caution flag on how cleanly this print can be read.
reverse_dcf_judgment: At ~120-155x trailing P/E and ~27-30x EV/EBITDA (source-dependent, all in the same extreme-rich zone) against ROE of 11-13% and ROCE of ~7.4-9%, the market is pricing sustained high-teens-to-20s% EBITDA/earnings compounding for many years with improving, not worsening, credit metrics. The current top-line trajectory (revenue/EBITDA +22-23% YoY, capacity +27-35% YoY) superficially supports that growth rate, but almost none of it is coming from retained cash flow - the company added ~2.5x FY26 EBITDA in net new debt to fund it, and a rising share of EBITDA growth is being absorbed by interest-cost growth (+18.9% YoY in Q4, ~46% of net sales) rather than flowing to the bottom line. A grid-evacuation ceiling that management admits caps additions well below its own capital capacity, combined with interest coverage barely above 1x, means the multiple is underwriting flawless multi-year execution with no room for setbacks - a bar this balance sheet cannot comfortably clear. Verdict: rich, not fair - the price assumes a smoother, less-levered compounding path than the FY26 numbers actually show. [Re-adjudicated 2026-07-20: our genuine 3y forward growth expectation (expected_next_3y_growth_pct) is therefore anchored well below that market-implied high-teens-to-20s% pace, at the ROE-implied sustainable growth rate of ~12% - what retained earnings can fund without further leverage deterioration - since the same coverage/curtailment constraints described above apply to our own forecast, not just to the market's].
